prompt: How does a goroutine end in Go?
hint: Section 02 says there is no handle to kill.

choices.text: Another goroutine stops it through its handle
choices.why: Go gives you no handle on a goroutine at all, so there is nothing to stop it through.

choices.text: Its function returns
choices.why: Right. Returning is the one way out, which is why a goroutine blocked forever is a goroutine forever.

choices.text: The garbage collector frees it once nothing refers to it
choices.why: The collector frees memory, not goroutines. The leak profile can report a stuck one; it does not end it.

choices.text: It times out after a while with no work
choices.why: There is no such timeout. The leaked goroutines of `first.go` waited for the whole run.

prompt: `first.go` reported 3 goroutines after one call and 203 after a hundred more. How many goroutines does each call to `first` leave behind?
In `first.go`, why are the goroutines for servers 2 and 3 stuck, while server 1's goroutine finished?
hint: Who is receiving on `ch` when each of them sends?

choices.text: Servers 2 and 3 sleep for ever, so they never reach the send
choices.why: They sleep 20 and 30 milliseconds. The sleep ends; the send after it never does.

choices.text: Their sends have no receiver, because `first` has already returned
choices.why: Right. An unbuffered send waits for a receiver, and the only one has gone.

choices.text: The channel was closed after the first answer
choices.why: Nothing closes `ch`. A send on a closed channel would panic, not wait.

choices.text: Three goroutines cannot share one channel
choices.why: Any number of goroutines may send on one channel; that part of the design is fine.

prompt: `early.go` ran `process` 100 times, 50 of them with an empty line, and ended with 51 goroutines. Which line's absence on the error path caused it?
hint: What ends a `for range` over a channel?

choices.text: `logs <- l`
choices.why: Skipping a send leaves the helper waiting for the next value, but it is the missing close that keeps it waiting forever.

choices.text: `chars += len(l)`
choices.why: That line is inside the helper and runs for every line it receives; it has nothing to do with how the helper ends.

choices.text: `close(logs)`
choices.why: Right. The early `return` jumps over it, and the helper's `for range` waits for a close that never comes.

choices.text: `_ = chars`
choices.why: That line only keeps the compiler from complaining about an unused variable.

prompt: A service leaks one goroutine per failed request. Each leaked goroutine holds a 64 KB buffer it was filling. What will the operators see first?
hint: A blocked goroutine uses no processor.

choices.text: Processor use climbing with every failed request
choices.why: A blocked goroutine is never scheduled, so it costs no processor time.

choices.text: Memory growing, never given back
choices.why: Right. The stacks and everything they reach, the buffers here, stay alive for as long as the goroutines do.

choices.text: A crash with a deadlock message
choices.why: The deadlock message appears when every goroutine is asleep. A server's other goroutines keep running.

choices.text: Failed requests answered more slowly
choices.why: The leak happens after the request has its answer; it does not slow the answer down.

prompt: What does the goroutine profile, printed with debug level 1, give that `runtime.NumGoroutine` does not?
hint: Look at the line `200 @ ...` and the line under it.

choices.text: A more exact total than the counter
choices.why: The total is the same, 201 in both.

choices.text: The memory each goroutine holds
choices.why: The profile shows stacks, not sizes. Memory is a different profile.

choices.text: Grouped stacks, with the line each group waits at
choices.why: Right: 200 goroutines at line 19 of `find.go` is the leak with its address.

choices.text: The time each goroutine has been waiting on its channel
choices.why: Debug level 1 shows no waiting times, only grouped stacks and counts.

prompt: Why is `main` listed in the `goroutine` profile of `find.go` but not in its `goroutineleak` profile?
hint: What does the leak profile try to prove about a goroutine?

choices.text: `main` is running, so nothing proves it will never run again
choices.why: Right. The leak profile lists only goroutines blocked on something no running goroutine can reach.

choices.text: The leak profile hides the main goroutine on purpose, by design
choices.why: There is no special case for `main`; a blocked `main` waiting on an unreachable channel would be stuck like any other.

choices.text: `main` had already returned
choices.why: When `main` returns the program ends, and nothing would be printed.

choices.text: Only goroutines started with `go` appear in it
choices.why: That is not the rule it applies. It reports goroutines it can prove are stuck.

prompt: `hidden.go` leaked 200 goroutines and its `goroutineleak` profile said `total 0`. What should a reader conclude from an empty leak profile in their own service?
hint: What kept the channel in `hidden.go` reachable?

choices.text: That the service has no leak and needs no further watching
choices.why: `hidden.go` is the counterexample: 200 leaked goroutines and a profile of zero.

choices.text: That the profile failed to run and printed nothing useful
choices.why: It ran: it printed its header and a total. It found nothing it could prove.

choices.text: No leak it could prove; the count still matters
choices.why: Right. A channel reachable from a global, or from anything alive, hides its waiters from the proof.

choices.text: That the leaked goroutines finished
choices.why: The same program printed `goroutines: 201` just before the profile.

prompt: The package that keeps the goroutine profile, and the leak profile beside it, is `runtime/___`.
Match each tool with the question it answers about a leak.
hint: From the cheapest to the most precise.

pairs.right: which line every goroutine is stopped at
which goroutines can provably never run again

right_distractors: how much processor time each goroutine used

prompt: What single change turned `first.go` into `buffered.go`, which ends a hundred calls with one goroutine?

choices.text: Receiving three times instead of once
choices.why: That would also stop the leak, but it waits for the slowest server, which defeats the point of `first`.

choices.text: A channel with room for three answers
choices.why: Right. No send ever waits, so every sender returns.

choices.text: Closing the channel after the first answer
choices.why: The later senders would then panic with a send on a closed channel.

choices.text: A `time.Sleep` in `main` before counting
choices.why: `first.go` already slept 100 ms before counting, and still counted 203.

prompt: `buffered.go` fixed the leak with `const servers = 3` used for both the buffer and the loop. What is the fragile part the section points out?
hint: What happens when somebody adds a server?

choices.text: Buffered channels cost more time per send than unbuffered ones
choices.why: The section says nothing about speed; its worry is correctness.

choices.text: The buffer keeps the answers in memory for ever
choices.why: The buffer is collected with the channel once nothing refers to it.

choices.text: The buffer's size has to keep matching the number of senders
choices.why: Right. A fourth sender with a buffer of three brings back one leaked goroutine per call.

choices.text: A constant cannot size a channel
choices.why: It can, and it did: `make(chan string, servers)` compiled and ran.

prompt: Why does `done.go` put `defer close(logs)` right after `make` rather than a `close(logs)` before each `return`?

choices.text: A deferred close is faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the two take the same work.

choices.text: It runs on every way out, later returns included
choices.why: Right. The leak in `early.go` was a `return` added beside the close and jumping over it.

choices.text: Closing a channel twice is allowed only with `defer`
choices.why: Closing twice panics however it is done; `done.go` closes once.

choices.text: Without `defer` the helper goroutine would never start
choices.why: The goroutine starts at the `go` statement either way.

prompt: Several goroutines each wait in a `select` on their send and on a channel `done`. What lets the owner stop all of them with a single statement?
hint: What does a receive on a closed channel do?

choices.text: Sending one value on `done`, which reaches every goroutine
choices.why: A value sent on a channel is received by exactly one receiver, so one send stops one goroutine.

choices.text: `close(done)`, which is ready for every receiver at the same time
choices.why: Right. A closed channel never blocks a receive, so every `select` sees it.

choices.text: Setting `done` to `nil`
choices.why: That changes the owner's variable; the goroutines hold their own copy of the channel and keep waiting.

choices.text: Calling `runtime.Goexit` from the owner
choices.why: `Goexit` ends the goroutine that calls it, the owner, not the others.

prompt: Put the section's three questions in the order to ask them before writing `go`.
hint: From what it blocks on to the caller giving up.
items: What happens if the caller gives up early?

prompt: Which of these goroutines can leak? Choose all that apply.
hint: For each, ask who completes the operation it blocks on.

choices.text: One sending its result on an unbuffered channel the caller may stop reading
choices.why: Yes: the `first.go` shape.

choices.text: One ranging over a channel that is closed only at the end of the happy path
choices.why: Yes: the `early.go` shape.

choices.text: One sending on a channel whose buffer has room for every sender
choices.why: No send waits, so it returns: `buffered.go`.

choices.text: One ranging over a channel closed by a `defer` right after `make`
choices.why: The close runs on every path: `done.go`.

prompt: A colleague fixes `first.go` by making it receive three times and return the first answer. The leak is gone. What did the fix cost?

choices.text: Nothing: same as the buffered version
choices.why: The buffered version returns after the fastest server; this one waits for all three.

choices.text: A goroutine per call, now leaked elsewhere
choices.why: With three receives every sender has a receiver, so none is left waiting.

choices.text: Each call now takes as long as the slowest server
choices.why: Right: 30 ms instead of 10. The point of asking three was to take the fastest.

choices.text: A panic when the third answer arrives
choices.why: Receiving three values from three senders is ordinary and does not panic.

prompt: A service built like `early.go` handles 2,000 requests an hour, and 3 in every 100 hit the early return. How many goroutines has it leaked after 10 hours?
